1
INTEREST OF AMICI CURIAE1

 Dee Deidre Farmer is an individual who experienced serious violations of her constitutional rights
by federal officers involved in domestic law enforcement. Ms. Farmer was the successful petitioner in
Farmer v. Brennan , 511 U.S. 825 (1994), where this
Court vacated the dismissal of her Bivens claim that
prison officials were deliberately indifferent in violation of the Eighth Amendment in failing to protect her
from sexual assault. Ms. Farmer has since co -authored a law review article discussing her experiences
behind bars following this Court’ s remand. She continues to support incarcerated people through her
nonprofit organization, Fight4Justice , and as a consultant to legal organizations that work on issues pertaining to gender equality . She graduated from
Georgetown University Law Center’s MORCA-
Georgetown Paralegal Program.

 The National Trans Bar Association (“NTBA”)
is a bar association formed by and for transgender and
gender non-conforming legal professionals, law school
students, and allies who care about transgender
rights. NTBA’s core mission is to support transgender
and gender non-conforming people in the legal profession and to increase the community’s access to affordable and culturally competent legal services. NTBA
also strives to secure formal legal protections for
transgender and gender non -conforming people to
meaningfully address issues of equity. NTBA has

1 Pursuant to Rule 37.6, amici confirm that no counsel for

2
hosted Ms. Farmer and other formerly incarcerated
transgender people at numerous Continuing Legal
Education panels and presentations for legal audiences.

 Bay Area Lawyers for Individual Freedom
(“BALIF”) is a bar association of legal professionals in
the San Francisco Bay Area —including judges, lawyers, law students, and legal workers—that envisions
a world where  lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender ,
queer, questioning, and intersex (“LGBTQI+”) people
live with dignity and equality under the law. BALIF’s
mission is to lead the LGBTQI+ legal community
through advocacy, justice, community empowerment,
and professional development and represent its members’ interests in the wider San Francisco Bay A rea.
As the nation’s oldest and largest LGBT bar association, BALIF  was founded in 1980 to encourage
LGBTQI+ legal professionals to apply to become
judges. At the time of BALIF’s founding, there were
no openly LGBTQI judges —today there are many.
BALIF’s mission has since expanded to take on questions of law and justice that affect the LGBTQI+ community.

 In the present case, the Court will decide how
its Bivens framework applies to claims from incarcerated people who report that prison officials deny necessary medical care with deliberate indifference. Such
claims involve constitutional violations by line -level
federal officers in ordinary prison administration ,
which fall squarely within the historical core of the
Bivens doctrine. The question presented adopts Petitioner’s assertion that this case presented “an alternative remedial scheme this Court did not consider in
Carlson” and “significant factual differences such as

3
the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged.”
Amici present the Court with Ms. Farmer’s case as a
standard application of Carlson that differed in both
the immediacy and severity of harm alleged but nevertheless was treated by this Court as a Bivens case.
Farmer demonstrates an application—not an extension—of Carlson that included a different degree of
immediacy and severity of harm, so long as the claims
are in the same legal context: deliberate indifference
to the health or safety of a person held in federal custody. Accepting Petitioner’s view —that the Carlson
context includes claims in which an incarcerated person died following an acute asthma attack that prison
officials not only failed to treat , but exacerbated,
Pet’r’s Br. 24–31—would effectively limit Carlson to
its facts. Amici argue that because this Court understood Ms. Farmer’s case to fit in the Carlson context,
Respondent’s claim fits in it, too . Accord Resp’t’s Br.
18–24.

4
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

 Mr. Watanabe’s medical claim falls within the
existing Bivens context established by Carlson v.
Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980). Accord Resp’t’s Br. 13–17.
Carlson provides a monetary damages remedy for
claims regarding the deliberate indifference of an individual federal prison official to a known, substantial
risk to the health or safety of an incarcerated person.
The severity of an injury does not create a new Bivens
context, as this Court’s decision in Farmer v. Brennan,
511 U.S. 825 (1994), makes clear.

 In Farmer, this Court held that ignoring an obvious risk of sexual assault in prison is an Eighth
Amendment violation that could be remedied by monetary damages. In reaching the merits of Ms.
Farmer’s failure -to-protect claim, the Court unmistakably understood the case as a Bivens case. A contrary conclusion finds no support in the text of the
opinion, the oral argument transcript, or the memoranda of the Justices . Farmer is a Carlson case. Accord Resp’t’s Br. 28. Courts construe failure-to-protect
claims and medical care claims using the same deliberate indifference standard. Threats to the health or
safety of an incarcerated person frequently overlap.

 Even under modern Bivens jurisprudence following Ziglar v. Abbasi, 582 U.S. 120 (2017), Hernández v. Mesa, 589 U.S. 93 (2020) , and Egbert v. Boule,
596 U.S. 482 (2022), the Bivens question has remained the same. Petitioner argues that a new alternative remedial scheme that Carlson did not consider
renders this case a new context. Pet ’r’s Br. 32 –35.
Carlson was decided after the federal courts had already seen the strong effects of the requirement to

5
exhaust the Bureau of Prisons’ administrative remedies before filing suit. And the severity of the injury
has no bearing on any of the most relevant factors pertaining to the question whether Congress should be
the governmental body to make a determination regarding the implied damages.

 Finally, public policy supports these claims because damages remedies provide crucial safeguards in
prisons.

ARGUMENT

I. THIS COURT ADJUDICATED  FARMER
AS A BIVENS ACTION.

 In Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of
Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971), this
Court “established that the victims of a constitutional
violation by a federal agent have a right to recover
damages against the official in federal court despite
the absence of any statute conferring such a right.”
Carlson v. Green , 446 U.S. 14, 18 (1980). Today, a
Bivens claim is shorthand for an implied damages
remedy against federal officers who violate the U.S.
Constitution. Within a decade following its decision in
Bivens, this Court found an implied damages remedy
in a Fifth Amendment gender discrimination case,
Davis v. Passman, 442 U.S. 228 (1979), and an Eighth
Amendment cruel and unusual punishment case,
Carlson, 446 U.S. at 14. In those three cases—Bivens,
Davis, and Carlson—this Court identified “two situations” that might “defeat [a Bivens cause of action] in
a particular case.” Id. at 18. First, when there are any
“special factors counseling hesitation in the absence of
affirmative action by Congress,” such as “a question

6
of ‘federal fiscal policy.’”  Id.; Bivens, 403 U.S. at 396
(quoting United States v. Standard Oil Co. , 332 U.S.
301, 311 (1947)); Davis, 442 U.S. at 245 . Second,
“when defendants show that Congress has provided
an alternative remedy which it explicitly declared to
be a substitute for recovery under the Constitution
and viewed as equally effective.” Carlson, 446 U.S. at
18–19 (emphasis in original); see also Bivens, 403 U.S.
at 397; Davis, 442 U.S. at 245–47.

 But very quickly after these cases were decided,
the Court began to retreat from finding implied damages remedies in new contexts based on concerns of
burdening and “overdeter[ring] federal officials and
undermin[ing their] ability to respond in times of
crisis.” James E. Pfander, Alexander A. Reinert &
Joanna C. Schwartz, The Myth of Personal Liability:
Who Pays When Bivens Claims Succeed, 72 Stan. L.
Rev. 561, 563 (2020). The Court’s more hesitant view
of the doctrine was articulated in Bush v. Lucas, 462
U.S. 367 (1983), in which the Court denied an implied
damages remedy in a First Amendment protected
speech retaliation claim brought by a federal government employee because of the “elaborate remedial
system” that Congress and the Executive Branch had
provided for remedying any violations against federal
employees. See id. at 385–90.

 In 1994, after the Court had already indicated
its hesitancy with implied damages remedies in Bush,
this Court issued its decision in Farmer v. Brennan ,
511 U.S. 825 (1994), which involved a claim seeking
damages and equitable relief under the Eighth
Amendment. The Court’s majority opinion clearly
stated that Ms. Farmer had filed “a Bivens complaint.” Id. at 830. In her lawsuit, Ms. Farmer alleged,

7
inter alia, that the Warden of her institution, her case
manager, the regional director, and the correctional
services administrator were responsible for the conditions and environment where she resided and was
transferred to, and were therefore deliberately indifferent to her safety.  Pl.’s First Am. Compl. for Damages & Injunctive Relief ¶¶ 1, 10–17, Farmer v. Brennan, No. 91-cv-716 (W.D. Wis. Dec. 13, 1991). Specifically, these defendants showed disregard for her
safety when they classified and placed her in a federal
penitentiary with a violent environment “knowing
such [placement] would endanger her life and indeed
did result in her being . . . sexually assaulted.” Id. ¶ 1.

 Ms. Farmer’s experiences that led to her complaint are harrowing. Upon incarceration, a psychologist employed by the federal Bureau of Prisons
(“BOP”) wrote a report that “noted that [Ms. Farmer]
would likely experience a number of difficulties during her incarceration, including a great deal of sexual
pressure because of her youth and feminine appearance.” Id. ¶ 39. As she was transferred to various BOP
facilities, officials were aware that she was at a risk
of harm in general population, so they kept her in segregation for her own protection. Id. ¶¶ 43–82, 87. After three years in segregation, BOP officials transferred her to a maximum -security facility—the U.S.
Penitentiary at Terre-Haute—where she was released
into general population. Id. ¶¶ 82, 87, 88. Although
the Petitioner and United States argue that prison -
administration concerns distinguish recent claims
from Carlson, Pet’r’s Br. 28–29, 39–40; U.S. Br. 12 –
15, the violations in Farmer involved classification,
transfer, protective segregation, institutional security, and placement in general population —all core
prison administrative decisions. Notably, Carlson

8
included administrative decisions, as well, given that
the decedent direly needed a transfer to a hospital
outside of the facility. Carlson, 446 U.S. at 16 n.1.

 A little over a week after being transferred  to
Terre-Haute and released into general population ,
Ms. Farmer was sexually assaulted by another incarcerated person. First Am. Compl. ¶ 89, Farmer, No.
91-cv-716. Ms. Farmer  has since shared in a published law review article that the person who assaulted her was “serving a life sentence for murder.”
Dee Deidre Farmer & D Dangaran, Farmer at 31: Historicizing Trans Rights in Prison Through Intergenerational Dialogue , 48 N.Y.U. Rev. L. & Soc. Change
321, 332 (2025). In that article, Ms. Farmer wrote:
“[He] came into my cell, beat me up, and raped me.”
Id. “[He] had a knife, and I was so fearful that he was
going to kill me that I could not tell him to stop.” Id.

 Based on the BOP officials’ decision to transfer
her despite their awareness of the “high probability
that she could not [safely] function” in Terr e-Haute’s
general population, First Am. Compl. ¶ 97, Farmer,
No. 91-cv-716, Ms. Farmer filed suit, arguing that she
had been denied “her Eighth Amendment right to be
free from deliberate indifference to her [safety] by the
Defendants[’] failure to provide for her [safety], protection and safekeeping.” Id. ¶ 101. She requested, inter alia, compensatory and punitive damages against
the aforementioned defendants. Id. ¶ 102. The district
court granted summary judgment to the defendants
for lack of requisite state of mind, finding they had “no
knowledge of any potential danger” to Ms. Farmer because she “never expressed any concern for [her]
safety to any of [them].” Farmer, 511 U.S. at 831–32.
The Seventh Circuit summarily affirmed. Id. at 832.

9
Ms. Farmer filed a pro se petition for certiorari that
essentially advocated for a recklessness standard to
the subjective component of her Eighth Amendment
claim. Pet. for Writ of Cert. at 10–17, Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825 (1994) (No. 92-7247).

 This Court’s opinion concluded that a plaintiff
has a viable Eighth Amendment claim “based on a
failure to prevent harm,” even where a plaintiff at obvious risk of harm did not directly notify prison officials of that risk. Farmer, 511 U.S. at 842–43, 848–49.
The Court adopted a criminal recklessness standard
for such cases and remanded to the district court for
further findings. Id. at 837–40, 848–51.

 Importantly, this Court understood that Ms.
Farmer was seeking damages under a Bivens theory.
See id.  at 830–31; 839 . It made no difference that
there may have been injunctive relief available to Ms.
Farmer; the Court still treated her Complaint as a
Bivens action. But see Pet’r’s Br. 25 –26, 30 –31, 34
(arguing that Bivens should only apply in a case of
“damages or nothing”); U.S. Br. 18, 21–23 (same). The
same logic should apply to Mr. Watanabe’s case. See
Resp’t’s Br. 21 –24. The Farmer opinion discussed
Ms. Farmer’s damages claim explicitly. See Farmer,
511 U.S. at 848, 850. The Court cited both Bivens and
Carlson when reciting Ms. Farmer’s allegations. See
id. at 830. This unequivocal understanding of the
case as a Bivens case aligns with the  consensus a t
oral ar gument, where Justice Ginsburg clarified
that this case is “a Bivens case.” See Oral Argument
at 24:50, Farmer v. Brennan, 511 U.S. 825 (1994) (No.
92-7247), https://www.oyez.org/cases/1993/92 -7247
[https://perma.cc/DZ3S-ZSDZ] (“But this was  . . . this
was . . . it’s a Bivens case, isn’t it?”) . Finally, during

10
deliberations, in a letter from Justice Ginsburg to Justice Souter and copied in a memorandum to the Conference, Justice Ginsburg wrote: “Although Bivens
provides the cause of action here, in many cases prisoners will be suing state officials under §1983 and alleging Eighth Amendment violations.” Memorandum
from Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg to Justice David H. Souter, Re: Farmer v. Brennan, No. 92-7247
(Mar. 9, 1994), in Papers of Harry A. Blackmun, No.
92-7247, https://clearinghouse.net/doc/136507/
[https://perma.cc/U8QZ-SNZX].

 The Court’s express identification of the complaint as a Bivens action, its discussion of damages liability, and its order vacating and remanding the
damages action are difficult to reconcile with treating
the claim as outside an established Bivens context.
Farmer, 511 U.S. at 830–31, 848, and 850–51. Indeed,
when the case was eventually tried before a jury, the
only claim remaining was the Bivens damages claim.
See Pl.’s Proposed Jury Instructions -Damages,
Farmer v. Brennan, No. 91-cv-716 (W.D. Wis. Jan. 8,
1997), Dkt. No. 170; Pl.’s Proposed Special Verdict -
Damages, Farmer v. Brennan , No. 91-cv-716 (W.D.
Wis. Jan. 8, 1997), Dkt. No. 172.

 Yet, lower courts that have rejected Farmer as
a Bivens context have stated—with no support—that
this Court in Farmer merely assumed without deciding that Ms. Farmer’s claim was a valid Bivens action
before proceeding to discuss the deliberate indifference standard. See, e.g., Sargeant v. Barfield, 87 F.4th
358, 365 (7th Cir. 2023) . But a close read of Farmer
shows that the Court never states that it merely assumes that it is reviewing a Bivens claim. This Court
has not listed Farmer alongside the three existing

11
Bivens contexts, but it also has never stated that
Farmer is not a Bivens context. Indeed, in Abbasi, this
Court left Farmer out of two lists collecting cases —
first, the trio of canonical Bivens cases, and second, an
extensive list of cases in which the Court had “declined to create an implied damages remedy.” Abbasi,
582 U.S. at 131–32, 135. But this Court has not decided sub silentio that Farmer is not a Bivens case.
Farmer was a groundbreaking case  that the Court
clearly understood as a Bivens case. The Court
reached the merits of the Eighth Amendment failureto-protect claim to discuss the deliberate indifference
standard only because it believed Ms. Farmer’s claim
was a viable Bivens action.

 A Third Circuit opinion agreed with this reasoning. In Bistrian v. Levi, 912 F.3d 79 (3d Cir. 2018),
the Third Circuit stated that “[a]lthough the Farmer
Court did not explicitly state that it was recognizing a
Bivens claim, it not only vacated the grant of summary judgment in favor of the prison officials but also
discussed at length ‘deliberate indifference’ as the legal standard to assess a Bivens claim.” Id. at 90–91.
The Third Circuit  was not deterred by the fact that
Abbasi listed only Bivens, Davis, and Carlson as the
established Bivens contexts “and did not address, or
otherwise cite to, Farmer.” Id. at 91. It “ decline[d] to
conclude that the Supreme Court’s more recent cases
have, by implication, overruled [Farmer].” Id. Instead,
it held that the failure-to-protect claim at issue in Bistrian did not present a new context because of its similarity to Farmer, allowing the damages claim to proceed. Id. at 90–92. Notably, Bistrian was decided after
this Court issued Abbasi, which stated that Bivens,
Davis, and Carlson “represent the only instances in
which the Court has approved of an implied damages

12
remedy under the Constitution itself.”  Abbasi, 582
U.S. at 131. This language did not persuade the Third
Circuit to reject failure -to-protect claims as Bivens
claims at the first step of the Bivens analysis—where
the canonical trio come into play.

II. FARMER IS IN THE SAME CONTEXT AS
CARLSON.

 The Supreme Court reached the merits of Ms.
Farmer’s Bivens claim without discussing whether
there was a valid Bivens cause of action because it had
already conducted that analysis in Carlson. There,
the Court framed the right at issue as “a violation of
the Eighth Amendment’s proscription against infliction of cruel and unusual punishment, giving rise to a
cause of action for damages under Bivens.” Carlson,
446 U.S. at 17 , 18–23. The specific allegations were
narrower than that formulation—though they contain
far more than simply exacerbating an asthma attack
that caused death. But see Pet’r’s Br. 25–31 (characterizing Carlson’s context as an acute, fatal medical
emergency); U.S. Br. 21 –23 (same);  States Br. 5
(same). The plaintiff claimed that the defendants
knew that the decedent had chronic asthma but nevertheless

kept him in [Terre Haute] against the
advice of doctors, failed to give him competent medical attention for some eight
hours after he had an asthmatic attack,
administered contra -indicated drugs
which made his attack more severe, attempted to use a respirator known to be
inoperative which further impeded his

13
breathing, and delayed for too long a
time his transfer to an outside hospital.

Carlson, 446 U.S. at 16 n.1. Like the plaintiff in Carlson, Ms. Farmer was placed in Terre Haute’s general
population against the advice of a doctor. First Am.
Compl. ¶ 39, Farmer, No. 91-cv-716. Unlike the plaintiff in Carlson, her case did not involve an acute medical event, but this Court nevertheless treated her
claim as a Bivens action. Thus, based on the Supreme
Court’s broad language stating the context of the case,
the remedy in Carlson should not be limited to medical deliberate indifference claims —and certainly not
only those arising from fatal medical emergencies —
but establishes damages action against federal officers for the deliberate indifference to health or safety,
more broadly. Accord Resp’t’s Br. 18 –23. Farmer
therefore reaffirms a reading of Carlson that the case
extends beyond instances of death ; cf. Pet’r’s Br. 18,
24–31; U.S. Br. 21–23; States Br. 5.

 By the time Farmer was decided, this Court
had described medical care and protection from violence from other incarcerated people as related conditions of confinement. See Wilson v. Seiter , 501 U.S.
294, 303 ( 1991) (“[ T]he medical care a prisoner receives is just as much a ‘condition’ of his confinement
as the food he is fed, the clothes he is issued, the temperature he is subjected to in his cell, and the protection he is afforded against other inmates .” (emphasis
added)). And at least one court of appeals had decided,
as early as 1980, that failure-to-protect claims were in
the same context as Carlson and thus were afforded a
Bivens remedy. Gillespie v. Civiletti, 629 F.2d 637, 642
(9th Cir. 1980).

14
 Such claims can be differentiated from another
category of Eighth Amendment claims: claims regarding the excessive use of force by prison officials.  See
Goldey v. Fields, 606 U.S. 942, 943–45 (2025) (per curiam) (holding that excessive force claims in prison
fall outside Carlson’s context) ; cf. Pet’r’s Br. 28, 32,
39–40 (discussing precedent holding that excessive
force claims in prison are not Bivens claims); U.S. Br.
10–18, 20, 26–27 (same). Excessive use of force claims
do not apply the deliberate-indifference standard, but
instead require plaintiffs to show that an officer's
force was applied “maliciously and sadistically for the
very purpose of causing harm.” Whitley v. Albers, 475
U.S. 312, 320–21 (1986) (citation omitted). This Court
has discussed the conditions-of-confinement claims in
a separate category juxtaposed to excessive use of
force claims. See id. at 319–21. Thus, the “deliberate
indifference to a prisoner’s serious illness or injury,”
id. at 320 (quoting Estelle v. Gamble, 429 U.S. 97, 105
(1976)), as well as deliberate indifference to “harsh
‘conditions of confinement,’” id. at 319 (quoting
Rhodes v. Chapman, 452 U.S. 337, 347 (1981)), have
been viewed differently from a “setting” in which
“competing obligations” of the prison officials caused
this Court to hesitate “to critique in hindsight decisions necessarily made in haste, under pressure, and
frequently without the luxury of second chance,” such
as the use of force applied “to resolve a disturbance”
in the facility, id. at 320. Accord Resp’t’s Br. 14, 29.

 For these reasons, Farmer does not arise in the
same context as Carlson merely because the two cases
are “based on the same constitutional provision.” Hernández v. Mesa, 589 U.S. 93, 103 (2020)  (“Hernández
II”); cf. Pet’r’s Br. 22–24, 30–31; U.S. Br. 11–12. There
are other claims based on the same constitutional

15
provision that do not receive the same legal treatment
whatsoever. Instead, as this Court stated in Farmer,
the two cases are both “prison -conditions cases,” in
which the Court must determine whether the defendants exhibited “deliberate indifference to inmate
health or safety.” Farmer, 511 U.S. at 834. The two
cases are brought by plaintiffs incarcerated in federal
prison against individual federal prison officials. They
raise claims regarding a known substantial risk to
health or safety that ordinary prison operations
should have remedied, seeking retrospective damages
to remedy harms that could not be undone —exacerbated physical conditions and the associated pain and
suffering. These claims go hand in hand because “[t]he
question under the Eighth Amendment is whether
prison officials, acting with deliberate indifference,
exposed a prisoner to a sufficiently substantial ‘risk of
serious damage to his future health.’” Id. at 843 (quoting Helling v. McKinney, 509 U.S. 25, 35 (1993)). Any
risk to a person’s safety is a risk to that person’s
health.

 Thus, as part of step one of the Bivens analysis,
the claim in Farmer should be understood as arising
in the same context as Carlson—deliberate indifference to a known, substantial risk to the health or
safety of a person in federal custody raised under the
Eighth Amendment. The context stated in this level
of generality—which was accepted by this Court—rebuts any narrower framing of Carlson to its facts. See
Pet’r’s Br. 22 –24; S tates Br. 6 –9. Although Farmer
involved different official conduct, a different form of
injury, a plaintiff who survived, and some prospective
relief raised alongside damages claims, the Court
acknowledged it as a Bivens case. Farmer undoubtedly falls under Carlson’s umbrella. As one Judge put

16
it: “the universal assumption in Farmer that a Bivens
remedy was available shows that the Court was treating failure -to-protect claims as fitting comfortably
within the reasoning of Carlson. That conclusion was
so obvious in Farmer that it did not need to be questioned or explained.” Sargeant, 87 F.4th at 371 (Hamilton, J., dissenting).

 Here, too, the Third Circuit previously agreed
with this reasoning. In Shorter v. United States , the
Third Circuit squarely placed Farmer in the Carlson
context rather than relying on Farmer as a standalone
Bivens context like the Bistrian court did. 12 F.4th
366, 373 n.5 (3d Cir. 2021) (“[T]he Supreme Court . . .
neglected to name Farmer because it saw that case as
falling under the umbrella of Carlson . . . .”); see also
id. at 371 (“In Farmer . . . the Supreme Court applied
Carlson in recognizing an Eighth Amendment damages claim.”).

 In 2024, however, the Third Circuit held that
Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022), abrogated its
precedents in Bistrian and Shorter. See Fisher v. Hollingsworth, 115 F.4th 197, 204 (3d Cir. 2024) (“Defendants respond that Bistrian and Shorter have been
abrogated by the Supreme Court’s later decision in
Egbert v. Boule. We agree.” (citation omitted)); see also
Kalu v. Spaulding , 113 F.4th 311, 329 –31 (3d Cir.
2024). Those decisions do not alter the historical point
demonstrated by Farmer itself: this Court understood
Ms. Farmer’s suit as a Bivens action and adjudicated
the governing Eighth Amendment standard on that
basis. The opinion, disposition, and contemporaneous
record therefore support treating Farmer as an application of Carlson’s established context, not an extension of Bivens into a new one.

17
III. BECAUSE FARMER IS A CLEAR APPLI-
CATION OF CARLSON, EVEN UNDER
THE MODERN BIVENS DOCTRINE, RE-
SPONDENT’S CLAIM IS ALSO AN APPLI-
CATION OF CARLSON.

 Differences in severity, immediacy, or ultimate
outcome of the delay or denial of serious medical
needs do not make Mr. Watanabe’s claim meaningfully different from Carlson, particularly in light of
Farmer. But see Pet’r’s Br. 22–23, 40–48. When Mr.
Watanabe suffered a fractured coccyx, prison medical
officials delayed his access to medical professionals
who could examine his pain as expert specialists.
Resp’t’s Br. 10. Delay was a core part of the facts in
Carlson. 446 U.S. at 16 n.1. Though Mr. Watanabe did
not die because of the delay, he did suffer immense
pain. Resp’t’s Br. 14, 23. These instances arise in the
same context—particularly because, from the defendant’s perspective, it is challenging to know what medical issue is actually capable of causing death. But see
Pet’r’s Br. 24 –32 (emphasizing that the prisoner in
Carlson died, creating a difference in the nature, severity, and immediacy of the injury there and in this
case); U.S. Br. 21–23 (arguing for a meaningful difference between a fatal asthma attack and Mr.
Watanabe’s nonfatal injury).

 But this Court has refused to limit Bivens, Davis, and Carlson “to the precise circumstances that
they involved.” Corr. Servs. Corp. v. Malesko, 534 U.S.
61, 75 (2001) (Scalia, J., concurring). But more to the
point, Farmer is a clear example that a Bivens case in
the Carlson context that evidences a seriously injurious harm that did not result in death could still be
grounds for a viable claim.

18
 Farmer is not part of an “ ancient regime” from
a time before extending the Bivens remedy became a
“disfavored judicial activity.” Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 131–
32 (discussing the bygone era of Bivens expansion
when “as a routine matter with respect to statutes,
the Court would imply causes of action not explicit in
the statutory text itself”) (quoting Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275, 287 (2001) )); Egbert, 596 U.S. at
491 (quoting Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 135 ). Despite Petitioner’s framing that Carlson belongs to an earlier,
more permissive era of implied causes of action, Pet’r’s
Br. 19–24, Farmer was decided after the Court had
already adopted a substantially more cautious approach to implied remedies.

 Ever since Bush v. Lucas was decided in 1983,
the Court had indicated its hesitation to step into legislative territory regarding the creation of implied
damages remedies. See 462 U.S. at 378–80, 388–90.
It’s true that the Supreme Court has “adopted a far
more cautious course before finding implied causes of
action” compared to the Court in Bivens, Davis, and
Carlson. Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 132. But that cautious
approach was already in effect during the Court’s
Farmer deliberations. Because Bush predates Farmer
by eleven years, Farmer cannot simply be characterized as a product of the bygone era of Bivens expansion. Petitioner’s account of  post-Carlson retrenchment fails to rebut the Court’s treatment of Farmer as
a Carlson-type Bivens claim; cf. Pet’r’s Br. 19–24; U.S.
Br. 23–28.

 The modern “ Bivens question . . . is ‘antecedent’ to the other questions presented,” Hernández v.
Mesa, 582 U.S. 548, 553 (2017)  (“Hernández I ”)

19
(quoting Wood v. Moss, 572 U.S. 744, 757 (2014)), and
therefore must be addressed before turning to the
merits of the claim. The Court has framed that inquiry in two steps. At step one, a court determines
whether the case presents a new Bivens context. Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 139. If the case is not meaningfully
different from Bivens, Davis, or Carlson, it does not
present a new context, and no extension of Bivens is
required. If, however, the court determines that the
case presents a new context, the court turns to step
two. At step two, the court assesses whether any special factors counsel hesitation before finding that “the
Judiciary is well suited, absent congressional action
or instruction, to consider and weigh the costs and
benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed. ” Id.
at 136.

 In Abbasi, the Supreme Court provided a non -
exhaustive “list of differences that are meaningful
enough to make a given context a new one:”

the rank of the officers involved; the constitutional right at issue; the generality
or specificity of the official action; the extent of judicial guidance as to how an officer should respond to the problem or
emergency to be confronted; the statutory or other legal mandate under which
the officer was operating; the risk of disruptive intrusion by the Judiciary into
the functioning of other branches; or the
presence of potential special factors that
previous Bivens cases did not consider.

Id. at 139–40. The Abbasi Court also identified special
factors relevant to the second  step, including

20
separation-of-powers principles (whether the judiciary is well suited to weigh the costs to the government, whether Congress has already acted in that
arena, etc.) and —of particular importance here—the
availability of alternative remedial structures. See id.
at 133 –37. Petitioner and the United States argue
that the Ninth Circuit erred by relegating alternative
remedial structures to step two. See Pet’r’s Br. 35–37;
U.S. Br. 11 –12. But Abbasi principally addressed alternative remedial structures as part of the special -
factors inquiry , and Egbert retained the two -step
framework while recognizing that the two inquiries
may overlap.

 Egbert—the case that caused the Third Circuit
to reconsider its precedent—did not abandon the Abbasi framework. Nor did it limit Bivens, Davis, and
Carlson “to the precise circumstances that they involved.” Malesko, 534 U.S. at 75 (Scalia, J., concurring). Instead, Egbert emphasized the rigor  of the
Bivens inquiry. The Egbert Court emphasized the judicial “caution” before recognizing a Bivens action.
596 U.S. at 491 (quoting Hernández II, 589 U.S. at
101). This Court recited the “two steps” framed by
precedent. Id. at 492. Then the Court stated: “While
our cases describe two steps, those steps often resolve
to a single question: whether there is any reason to
think that Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy.” Id. The Court further identified alternative remedial structures as a special factor
that can foreclose a Bivens remedy. Id. at 492–93.

 Although the Egbert Court indicated that the
two-step inquiry may “often resolve to a single question,” id. at 492–93, the Court applied the two discrete
steps of the Abbasi framework, see id.  at 494 –501.

21
Petitioner relies on Egbert to argue that the framework has collapsed into a single inquiry. Pet ’r’s Br.
22–24, 35–39. But as Respondent argues, Egbert did
not abolish the threshold new -context inquiry, and
Petitioner’s approach would “eliminate the first step
entirely.” Resp’t’s Br. 31–32. The core separation -ofpowers concern emphasized in  Egbert has been part
of the doctrine for decades. See Bush, 462 U.S. at 371–
72, 381 –90. Fo r instance, Egbert’s inquiry  into
whether the Judiciary or Congress is “better equipped
to create a damages remedy,” Egbert, 596 U.S. at 493,
has been a central part of the doctrine from before
Carlson was decided. See Bush, 462 U.S. at 380 (“The
special factors counselling hesitation in the creation
of a new remedy .  . . related to the question of who
should decide whether such a remedy should be provided.”); see also Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 135 (“When a
party seeks to assert an implied cause of action under
the Constitution itself, . . . separation-of-powers principles are or should be central to the analysis. The
question is ‘who should decide’ whether to provide for
a damages remedy, Congress or the courts?” (quoting
Bush, 462 U.S. at 380). This “single question” is useful
for understanding the “principles” at play, Egbert, 596
U.S. at 493, but it has not replaced the well-worn twostep inquiry. Most importantly, the Supreme Court
has declined to “dispense with Bivens altogether.” Id.
at 491. The special-factors analysis in Bivens step two
has always been to assess if there is “even a single
‘reason to pause before applying Bivens in a new context.’” Id. at 492 (quoting Hernández II, 589 U.S. at
102). The Bivens inquiry investigates whether any
factors counsel courts to defer to Congress, not
whether the factors weigh for or against finding an
implied damages claim . See Wilkie v. Robbins , 551
U.S. 537, 562 (2007); Bush, 462 U.S. at 389 –90.

22
Abbasi held that the “proper balance is one for the
Congress, not the Judiciary, to undertake.”  582 U.S.
at 146. Thus, Egbert did not diverge from Abbasi at
all by holding that courts cannot “independently assess the costs and benefits of implying a cause of action.” See Egbert, 596 U.S. at 495 (reversing a decision
that (1) weighed the costs of the new Bivens claim and
the compelling interests and (2) determined a damages remedy was implied).

 Egbert sent shock waves across the circuit
courts. The Third, Fourth, Seventh, and Ninth Circuit
courts of appeals have read Egbert as materially modifying the Bivens inquiry. See Fisher, 115 F.4th at 204
(“Egbert tightened the Ziglar test and, in doing so,
made a strong statement that lower courts should not
extend Bivens beyond the contexts recognized in
Bivens, Davis, and Carlson.”); Kalu, 113 F.4th at 330
n.10 (“Hernández [II] and Egbert evince the Court’s
new appreciation of ‘the tension between judicially
created causes of action and the Constitution’s separation of legislative and judicial power.’” (quoting Egbert, 596 U.S. at 491) (internal quotation marks omitted)); Bulger v. Hurwitz , 62 F.4th 127, 139 (4th Cir.
2023) (“[T]he Third Circuit did not have the benefit of
the Court’s more recent Bivens guidance, as Bistrian
was decided before the Court’s decisions in Hernández
and Egbert, both of which also list Bivens, Carlson,
and Davis as the only three cases in which the Court
has implied a Bivens action.”) (emphasis in original);
Sargeant, 87 F.4th at 364 (calling Egbert “most significant to this appeal” and holding it “modified the Abbasi approach”); Marquez v. Rodriguez, 81 F.4th 1027,
1030 (9th Cir. 2023) (“In practice, the Supreme
Court’s stringent test will foreclose relief in all but the
most extraordinary cases.” ). These courts read too

23
much into Egbert, which emphasized the restrictiveness of the Bivens inquiry but did not eliminate the
two-step framework. 596 U.S. at 492 . Any additional
stringency is merely dicta. The two -step inquiry is
still binding.

 Nor did Egbert overrule Farmer, which remains
good law. Amici contend that the Court’s adjudication
of the Bivens claim in Farmer demonstrates that an
Eighth Amendment failure -to-protect claim falls
within, rather than extends, the Carlson context.

 Petitioner argues that alternative remedies
available in Respondent’s case were not considered in
Carlson. Pet’r’s Br. 32–39. But administrative remedies for individuals in federal  custody existed in the
BOP’s rules and regulations well before the death at
issue in Carlson. See, e.g., Green v. United States, 283
F.2d 687, 688–89 (3d Cir. 1960) (describing BOP regulations permitting plaintiffs to seek review of local
prison officials’ actions directly from the Director of
the BOP through the “Prisoner’s Mail Box”)); Smoake
v. Willingham , 359 F.2d 386, 38 8 (10th Cir. 1966)
(same); Tarlton v. United States, 429 F.2d 1297, 1298
(5th Cir. 1970) (remanding to determine whether petitioner exhausted administrative remedies by writing to the Surgeon General, the Attorney General, and
the Director of the BOP regarding the denial of medical care). Moreover, as Respondent argues, Carlson
considered the Federal Tort Claims Act (“FTCA”), 28
U.S.C. §§ 1346(B), 2671  et seq., and held that it did
not displace the constitutional damages remedy. 446
U.S. at 18 –23; Resp’t’s Br. 6. The Administrative
Remedy Program (“ARP”) does not itself provide damages; it merely channels tort claims into the FTCA’s
procedures. See 28 C.F.R. § 542.10(c); Resp’t’s Br. 25–

24
26. Thus, the availability of administrative recourse
for incarcerated plaintiffs is not a post-Carlson development, contrary to the United States’s argument
here. See U.S. Br. 17–21.

 When Congress enacted the Prison Litigation
Reform Act (PLRA) in 1996, it did not abrogate Bivens
claims. See 42 U.S.C. § 1997e(e) (permitting prisoners
to bring civil actions for physical injury or the commission of a sexual act and resulting harms); McCarthy v. Madigan, 503 U.S. 140, 149–56 (1992) (holding
that a federal prisoner pursuing a Carlson claim was
not required  to exhaust the BOP’s administrative
grievance procedure before seeking monetary damages); accord Resp’t’s Br. 16. Rather, the PLRA creates procedural limitations such as the “exhaustion
requirement”—the rule that incarcerated plaintiffs
must utilize the full internal grievance procedure of
their prison system, including appealing any denials
in the first instance, bef ore they can bring a lawsuit
in federal court —to deter frivolous claims, including
frivolous Bivens actions, not prevent those claims altogether. See 141 Cong. Rec. H14105 (daily ed. Dec. 6,
1995) (statement of Rep. Lo Biondo) (discussing the
continued validity of Bivens claims but advocating for
an administrative exhaustion requirement in the
PLRA to deter frivolous Bivens actions); 42 U.S.C. §
1997e(a) (PLRA’s exhaustion provision); see also Porter v. Nussle, 534 U.S. 516, 524–25 (2002) (holding the
ARP is an exhaustion requirement for a Bivens claim
rather than a substitute for one). This legislative history demonstrates that Congress specifically regulated the relationship between prison litigation and
administrative remedies rather than replacing federal constitutional damages actions or statutory tort

25
actions with the administrative remedial program.
See Resp’t’s Br. 16.

 The Petitioner’s argument seems to simply apply the alternative remedies factor from the case law
without taking the larger context or goals of the factors into consideration . See Abbasi, 582 U.S. at 148.
But one of the key goals of the step two analysis is to
ensure deference to congressional intent. See id.  at
137; see also Wilkie, 551 U.S. at 550, 562. All evidence
points to the conclusion that Congress did not close off
Bivens claims in this context. See Federal Employees
Liability Reform and Tort Compensation Act of 1988
(Westfall Act), Pub. L. No. 100 -694, 102 Stat. 4563,
4564 (1988)  (codified as amended at 28 U.S.C. §
2679(b)(2)(A)) (noting that while the FTCA  would be
the exclusive remedy for common -law tort claims
against federal employees, those actions brought
against a federal employee “for a violation of the Constitution of the United States” would not be barred);
Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 111 n.9 (explaining the
Westfall Act “left Bivens where it found it); Hui v. Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799, 807 (2010) (discussing “[t]he
Westfall Act’s explicit exception for Bivens claims).
Taken together, the PLRA and the Westfall Act provide substantial evidence  that Congress did not intend for the BOP’s administrative grievance process
to displace Bivens remedies in this context.

 Further, Congress passed the PLRA less than
two years after Farmer was decided, and thus it understood that federal prisoners might bring failure-toprotect Bivens claims. See Lorillard v. Pons, 434 U.S.
575, 580–81 (1978) (holding Congress is presumed to
legislate with knowledge of Supreme Court decisions);
accord Resp’t’s Br. 28 (noting that PREA cited Farmer

26
and stating that Farmer “is a Carlson case”). Farmer’s
acceptance and use by Congress ’s express invocation
of Farmer in the Prison Rape Elimination Act
(“PREA”) demonstrates Congress’s understanding
that the Court had created constitutional damages
remedies for incarcerated people, which the PLRA
sought to structure procedurally, rather than limit
substantially. Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003
(“PREA”), Pub. L. No. 108 -79, § 2(13), 117 Stat. 972,
973 (codified at 34 U.S.C. § 30301(13)); accord Resp.
Br. 28 (noting that PREA  cited Farmer and stating
that Farmer “is a Carlson case”).

 Petitioner’s argument, repeated by the United
States, that the PLRA and other post-Carlson legislation are special factors is thus unfounded. See Pet’r’s
Br. 33–35; U.S. Br. 15–17. Carlson remedies have existed for more than forty-five years and have been understood by Congress and the courts to be a necessary
deterrent to harmful actions of individual federal officers. “[C]ongressional silence in the PLRA about the
availability of Bivens remedies does not suggest that
Congress intended to make such remedies unavailable.” Bistrian, 912 F.3d at 92 –93. The Bivens landscape against which Congress enacted the  PLRA in
1996 already included Farmer. If Congress ’s legislation fixed the p ermissible scope of Bivens claims
brought by people in federal custody,  amici contend
that those limits would still encompass failure-to-protect claims.

 Similarly, when Congress amended the FTCA
to cover law -enforcement torts in 197 4, it rejected a
proposal to eliminate Bivens actions in favor of suits
against the federal government and expressly articulated that these causes of action should operate in

27
parallel. See Carlson , 446 U.S. at 19 –20. Congress
subsequently legislated against the backdrop of the
Bivens framework, particularly in the prison context,
preserving constitutional claims in the Westfall Act
and imposing procedural limitations through the
PLRA. See Resp’t’s Br. 16 –17 (providing legislative
history of the Westfall Act, the FTCA, and the PLRA).
Congress later expressly cited Farmer in PREA when
describing the Eighth Amendment protections available to incarcerated people. See Resp’t’s Br. 28; 34
U.S.C § 30301(13).

IV. THIS COURT’S CONTINUED RECOGNI-
TION OF CARLSON CLAIMS PROTECTS
PUBLIC INTERESTS.

 On a structural level, i t is “unthinkable” that
the U.S. Constitution would hold states to a higher
standard than the federal government. Bolling v.
Sharpe, 347 U.S. 497, 500 (1954). But that is precisely
what this Court’s recent precedent requires. See Hernández II, 589 U.S. at 102 –05; Malesko, 534 U.S. at
68–74, Egbert, 596 U.S. 491 –93; 498.  Due to this
Court’s Bivens doctrine, state officials can be held accountable for constitutional violations brought in actions under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 even if those very same
violations would not give rise to an equivalent remedy
against a federal official. See Marquez, 81 F.4th at
1035–36 (Fletcher, J., concurring). One judge has
called this reality “a miscarriage of justice.” Id. at
1036. This Court does not need to do the “unthinkable.” Bolling, 347 U.S. at 500. For far too long, “the
Bill of Rights [has] monitor[ed] more closely the conduct of state officials than it does that of federal officials.” Butz v. Economou, 438 U.S. 478, 504 (1978). To
do so “is to stand the constitutional design on its

28
head.” Id. This Court need not perpetuate that remedial asymmetry here. Acknowledging Farmer and upholding Carlson is a much less drastic approach than
overruling Bivens. Cf. Pet’r’s. Br. 40; Mittleman Br. 9–
10. Amici and the Respondent ask only to continue to
apply Carlson within the established Bivens context,
not to extend Bivens to a new context. See Resp’t’s Br.
13–17, 33.

 And on a personal level, the stakes for incarcerated transgender people have never been higher. According to a report from the Bureau of Justice Statistics that measured the prevalence of sexual victimization in prisons via surveys conducted in 2007, 2008 –
09, and 2011 –12, more than 34% of transgender
adults incarcerated in state and federal prison su ffered sexual victimization, and 16.7% have been subject to staff sexual misconduct. Allen J. Beck, Bureau
of Justice Statistics, U.S. Dep’t of  Just., Sexual Victimization in Prisons and Jails Reported by Inmates,
2011-12: Supplemental Tables: Prevalence of Sexual
Victimization Among Transgender Adult Inmates  2,
tbls. 1– 2 (2014). In 2025, President Trump issued an
Executive Order setting a federal government
agenda to end any discussion of gender, gender identity, or sex that differed from the view that there are
only two biologically determined sexes: male and female. See Exec. Order 14168, 90 Fed. Reg. 8615 ,
8615–17 (Jan. 30, 2025). The BOP complied with the
order early on —before passing any regulations that
would execute the Executive Order —by preventing
transgender people from being housed according to
their gender identity, requiring them instead to be
housed according to their sex assigned at birth, and
quickly ending access to gender -affirming care such
as hormone therapy. Jaclyn Diaz, Federal Prisons

29
Prep to Move Trans Inmates as Early as This Week, NPR
(Feb. 25, 2025), https://www.npr.org/2025/02/21/nx-s1-
5305282/trans-inmates-federal-prison-policy-transfers
[https://perma.cc/6CXF-UDES]. Litigators challenged
these early administrative actions as unconstitutional
violations of the Eighth Amendment, see Doe v.
McHenry, 763 F. Supp. 3d 81, 87–89 (D.D.C. 2025), and
as violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, see
Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691, 2025 WL 1568238,
at *8–11 (D.D.C. June 3, 2025).

 While injunctions against BOP’s earlier implementation measures remained in place, BOP issued a
new policy in February 2026 that substantially preserved the same near total ban of gender-affirming
care and effectively eliminated safe placement accommodations or transgender people in federal custody.
U.S. Dep’t of Just., Fed. Bureau of Prisons, Program
Statement: 5260.01, Management of Inmates with
Gender Dysphoria 7–8 (Feb. 19, 2026). A district court
subsequently enjoined enforcement of this policy and
stayed its implementation under 5 U.S.C. § 705. See
Kingdom v. Trump, No. 25-cv-691, 2026 WL 1746251,
at *1 3–14 (June 17, 2026). The injunctive relief
granted by the district courts in this ongoing litigation
may prevent future harm, but it cannot compensate
for constitutional injuries that we have already suffered from. For those incarcerated transgender people
who have already suffered harm —akin to the harms
Ms. Farmer suffered—damages may be the only remedy capable of redressing the completed injuries .
Damages are a significant tool for ensuring federal officers meet the constitutional minimum requirements
for safety and health. Indeed, for some trans gender
people subjected to completed constitutional

30
violations, “it is damages or nothing.” Bivens, 403 U.S.
at 410 (Harlan, J., concurring).

CONCLUSION

 For the foregoing reasons, the judgment of the
court of appeals should be affirmed.
